concept.name: AR model
concept.definition: A time-series model in which the current value is expressed as a linear combination of its own p previous values plus a white-noise innovation. It is a linear regression of the series on its own lags and is stationary when the roots of its characteristic polynomial lie outside the unit circle.
concept.intuition: An AR model says today is explained by momentum or mean-reversion from the recent past: how much of yesterday (and the days before) carries into today.
concept.mechanics: An AR(p) model X_t = delta + phi_1*X_{t-1} + ... + phi_p*X_{t-p} + A_t is fit by linear least squares or maximum likelihood; the order p is identified from the PACF cutoff and information criteria. Its ACF decays gradually while its PACF cuts off after lag p. Stationarity requires the coefficients to satisfy constraints (e.g., |phi_1| < 1 for AR(1)).
concept.formula: X_t = delta + phi_1*X_{t-1} + ... + phi_p*X_{t-p} + A_t, where delta = (1 - sum phi_i)*mu with mu the process mean, and A_t white noise.
concept.failure_modes: Pure AR structure cannot capture shock-driven dynamics that need MA terms; wrong order selection underfits (residual autocorrelation) or overfits (poor out-of-sample forecasts). AR coefficients estimated on trending or non-stationary data are biased toward spurious persistence.
concept.misconceptions: That a high R-squared in an AR regression of a price level indicates forecasting power - levels regressions on near-unit-root data are misleading; returns-based AR models for stocks show little exploitable linear predictability.
concept.example: An AR(2) fitted to monthly industrial production uses the two previous months' values to forecast the next, with the PACF showing significant spikes at lags 1 and 2.

citations.source: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, Section 6.4.4.4 Common Approaches to Univariate Time Series
